A COWARDLY RUFFIAN AND THE CAT. A prisoner in Newgate, named William Leonard, re- ceived twenty lashes with the " cat " on Friday. He had robbed a young lady, with violence, in Lincoln's Inn Fields, and as he had been flogged in 1870 for a similar offence, he was ordered to suffer two floggings of twenty lashes each, at an interval of a month. The prisoner behaved in a cowardly manner, howling before be was struck, and shrieking the whole time. Besides the double flogging, he has to undergo seven years of penal servitude.

The London correspondent of a Liverpool contem- porary says—" The Times has done rather a venture- some thing in publishing the letter from Mr. Royes Bell which appears in that journal of Saturday. Mr. Bell says, in language which there can be no mis- taking, that Mr. Bravo was murdered, and that Mrs. Cox was the murderess. He attempts to disprove the theory of suicide, but not, I think, with success. Cer- tainly, so far as I have been able to gather, that theory is the one usually adopted, and is the only one consistent with the evidence. There is one thing to be said for Mr. Bell—he has at least the courage of his opinions. He says plainly whom be means when he talks of murder, although he may be called upon to make good his statement in a court of law: The Coroner's jury was under no such obligation, yet it brought in a verdict of murder without having the fairness to say which of the three possible criminals it meant to accuse. We have now to see what course Mrs. Cox will take in order to clear herself from the terrible charge which is so definitely made agAinst her. : I •

The spread of small-pox at Blackburn occasions considerable anxiety. At present there are 16 patients In the temporary hospital that has been erected on the workhouse grounds at Brandy House Brow, In addi- tion to this number, the sanitary authorities have under their care nine other cases. These are persons who are at their own homes, but it is known that there are many other cases that have not been reported to the authorities. From the Manchester Critic. A short time ago we noticed the commencement, in the Warrington Examintr, of a series of articles on "Liberal Legislation in the Nineteenth Century." The third paper on the subject appears in the current number, and continues its interesting sketch of Thomas Walker, the Manchester Liberal, who received the high distinction of being called by the Tory organ of his day an insidious viper, whose object was to "make one general wreck of the happiness of the empire." It describes graphically an onslught made by a Tory mob on the publishing office of the Manchester Liberal paper, the Herald. . The conduct of constables and magistrates in fomenting and encouraging the attack, as here related, gives us a pleasing idea of the im- partiality of the powers that were. After sacking the publishers, the enlightened majority proceeded to smash Mr. Walker's windows; but then, as the clerk to the magistrates, when appealed to, calmly observed, "it was a scandalous, shameful, and abominable busi- ness to call out the magistrates on such trifling busi- ness as the breaking of a few windows." The Tory party subsequently tiumped up against Walker a aharge of conspiracy to overthrow the Government, the refutation of which cost him £3,000, and left Lim "a marked and shunned man." Such was the reward for holding advanced opinions eighty years ago. Perhaps it's hardly safe to throw many stones at eighty years ago, though.
THE NEW POLLUTION OF RIVERS ACT.

The new Act for making further provision for the prevention of the pollution of rivers (39 and 40 Vic. cap. 75) has just been printed. The principal object of the statute, as declared by the preamble, is "to prevent the establishment of new sources of pollution." There are 22 sections, divided into six parts. The first re- lates to prohibiting the putting of solid matters into Streams, the next as to sewage pollutions, then as to manufacturing and mining pollutions. The fourth part has reference to the administration of the law, and sanitary authorities are to afford facilities for fac- tories draining into sewers, and those authorities have power to enforce the statute as also the Lea Conser- vancy Board. The other provisions relate to legal proceedings, Eze. Offences are to be restrained by summary orders of county courts, with the right of ap- peal to the high court of justice. The inspectors of the Local Government Board have similar powers as the inspectors under the Public Health Act of last year. They are to give certificates 88 to the best practi- cable means for rendering harmless any sewage matter falling or flowing into any stream. There are provi- sions as te the execution of the new law in ticotland and Ireland. Under this act, sanitary authorities and the Local Government, by active exertions, may pre- Tent the pollution of rivers.

A GAPING ADVENTURE AT BARNTGN, OILESHIRE.

The notorious dulness of our Cheshire Tillages and the listlessness especially inspired by a rural Sunday, f, as by law established," was curiously—not to say fearfully and wonderfully—illustrated at the village of Bunton on Sunday evening last. We trust we violate to confidence in stating that Mr. John Buckley— Bomwhat vaguely described as " a person from VVales" —being on a visit to his friends at Barnton, was sud- denly seized with a terrible fit of yawning. The pro- cess of yawning, is known in the vernacular cf Lancashire and Cheshire as "gaping." Mr. John, Buckley "the person from Wales" seems to be one of those terribly earnest gentlemen who never do anything by halves, and it appears that even When he 4' gapes " he gapes with sincerity and en- - - - •

thusiasm. -Mi. Buckley's gape—as one may say— goes the whole hog" his exalted ideal being apparently founded on a nice little quarry, or an infant salt mine in the immediate vicinity of the ' Village of Barnton. At any rate 'the person from Wales," established a gull upon his honest open countenance, sweetly suggestive to the meditative or scientific observer of new possibilities in Vivisec- tion, or some wilder romance than usual to be evolved 11 the law of Development. The fact is, that although Ms. Buckley didn't exactly (as the phrase goes) " lose his head," as he Raped so gigantically, the upper half of it temporarily disappeared. Literally, to quote our informant, Whilst in the act of gaping, Mr. Buckley " uncoupled his jaw," In a word, he opened his mouth so wide that his jaws were dislocated I Horrified at the re- sult of his determination to gape impressively, the startled gaper took to his heels and fled through the 1 Village—his gape flying with him, and retaining no. I disturbed its affectation of immovable astonishment— to the nearat doctor. We are not informed how Mr. Brickley contrived to explain his inarticulate yet ex• ceedingly open-mouthed condition to the esteemed and startled medical practitioner, who happened to be relieving the tedium of the day with "The Diversions ' Of Purley," but it may be that in these matters a wink hi as good as a nod to a doctor. butfice it to say, that under the auspices of the local Esculapius, the sePerated upper and lower jaws of Mr. Buckley came together again, their proprietor having resolved for the future to "hold his jaw" with greater circumspection. One would like to know the secret Of Mr. Buckley's extravagant gaping. It couldn't have been any sermon or sermons preached by any. body at Baruton ? There is not a Rector or Vicar in the county of Cheater equal to the exploit of preach- ing the half of a man's head a I It is equally diffi- cult to suppose that the " person hem Wales" had been reading all day in one of the local newspapers distinguished for its 'Neutrality." That experiment Would have remitted in a coroner's inquest! "Six days shalt thou labour" ? The Sabbath should be Sacred from the more than Egyptian drudgery in- evitable to him who essays laboriously to IsPell over that huge and melancholy broadsheet. Was Mr. Buckley suddenly fascinSted with the notion of obtaining University laurels loom Greenville d and, knowing that those learned backwoodsmen are "always on the prowl" for remarkable "Britishers " to whom they can sell their curiously honorary scalps and feathers, had determined byway of graduating for the distinction to " invent " a gape of such preter- natural dimensions as should correspond with the not less preternatural dulness of the great Greenville original in Warrington. We mustn't omit to mention that Mr. Buckley's surgical Experiment cost him a guinea, and that he shakes his head very negatively 'When a neighbouring musican with sly yet allusive inaccuracy exclaims 1)a G ape.

div.head: LOSING A CHESHIRE MAIL CART.
div.p: LOSING A CHESHIRE MAIL CART.

At the Nantwich Police ;Court, on Tuesday, Ben. jmnin Wynn was brought up in custody, with his head plastered, cbarged with being drunk in charge of a mail cart the previous day. Mr. Wood, postmaster, appeared to prosecute. From the evidence, it ap- peared that Wynn was employed to drive the mail cart carrying the bags between Crewe, Nantwich, and Whitchurch, and that shortly before two a.m. on Mon- day eleven bags were handed to him at Crewe station by a messenger, who stated that ue was " vei y tipsy." About four o'clock Wynn reached Nantwich, and knocked up the postmaster, asking him whether he had received the mail yet. When that offici4l ropli in the negative, Wynn, without stating any particlS." lan, told him he could go to bed again, as he had lost the cart. Intelligence shortly afterwards reached Crewe that the cart and horse, the former upset, had been found at Chesterton in Staffirdshire. The bags had been thrown into a hedge. It appeared that the driver had been thrown out on the road, and had found his way to Nantwich—quite in the opposite direction to that taken by his horse. The magistrates re. safanded Wynn until Saturday.

THE LAW AND INFECTIOUS DISEASES.

_ At the Eddisboy Petty Sessions, on Monday, Ellen Ellison, a married woman, living at Moss Bank, Over, was summoned for obstructing an officer of the Wins- ford Local Board of Health in ,the performance of his duty. Mr. Fletcher prosecuted, and Mr. Dixon ap- peared for the defence. Mr. Fletcher stated that pro- ceedings were taken under the 124th section of the which provided for the removal of Public Health Act, persons affected with any infectious distemper to a place of suitable accommodation, when, upon the cer- tificate of a doctor and the order of a justice, such re- 'novel was necessary. About the 23rd June, the de- fendant's husband and one of her sons were seized sanVar a with smallpox. and upon the certificate of Dr. Fraser the sanitary officer, Mr. B. Oakes., procured an order' from the Mayor of Over, Mr. Lewis, for their being to the workhouse hospital at Leftwich, there removal danger of the infection spreading. The officer, pursuant to the order, and after giving the 4,7 fendant notice, came to her house next morning with a van for the purpose of taking the patients to Left- wich. Defendant, however, refused to open the door, saying he would have to take her first; and he there- upon produced the Mayor's order, and read to her the 124th section of the Act. (Laughter.) This, however, f tiled to move her, and no was obliged to return to Northwich with his van. Three days after Mrs. Ellison was seized with the disease, and proceedings had in consequence been postponed. Mr. Dixon, in addres- sing the Bench, urged that his client acted in ignorance of the law. Mr. Fletcher did not doubt that ; but, he added, it was very important that the officers of health should not be obstructed, and people of this class wanted edueating up to these sanitary acts.—The Bench imposed a fine of ss. and costs, and informed the defendant that she had rendered herself liable to a penalty of £lO.

div.head: ROW AT THE RECTORY
div.p: ROW AT THE RECTORY
OF ASHTON-ON-MERSEY.

At Sale Sessions, on Monday, James Cartwright was summoned for assaulting Mary Brant, at Ashton-upon- Mersey, on the 26th July, Mr. Hockin;of Manchester prosecuted, and Mr. Brown defended. There was a cross-summons, Cart wright against Brant. Mr. Hockin in introducing the case for the prosecu- tion, said that he had to bring before the bench a cowardly and disgraceful assault committed by a per- eon who termed himself a man, upon an unprotected and defenceless woman. He trusted, that if he made good his case the bench would pass such a sentence as would not only !thew the defendant, hat others who were likely to be called upon to play the ruffian, that they as the administrators of justice, would not for a moment allow females to be assaulted as that young woman had been. On the 28th July the com- plainant was cook in the service of the Rev. Joseph Ray, the rector of Ashton-upon-Mersey, and the de- fendant was at the time, and is still the gardener in the employ of Mr. Ray. On the day of the assault Mr. Ray was not at home, and the:house was occupied by Mts. Ray, the complainant, and a fellow eervant, and the defendant, who was the only man on the premises. Therefore the defendant wsa the master of the position and he should show the bench the way he used that power and strength. It was his duty to supply vege- tables to the cook daily, and he was asked by her to supply her with potatoes. He brought them into the kitchen and being vexed at the order being given by her, said "I don't believe you want them but for your own purposes." That aroused the anger of the com- plainant, who told defendant that she and a fellow servant had seen him going away with a basket of vegetables. He seized her by the throat and ran her against the wall, held her there until she was nearly strangled—until her mouth was full of blood— After this he released her for an instant, and she seized the nearest thing at hand, a " jock " which she " shied "at him. The delete' snt then knocked her down, and sttuek her several violen', blows in the face. She ran away and was followed oy the defendant, who again eeized her and knocked her down again and again. The complainants screams brought into the kitchen Mrs. Ray and the other servant, and they saw the complainant on the fl mr, and saw the defendant strike her. She believing the man was in the wrong at once ordered him from the house. The complainant on the return of the master some days after complained and he held an investigation in his study, and asked them to forgive one another. That was all very nice and very pleasant, and the rector probably thought it was his duty to preach peace to not only his congrega• tion, but his household. He did not think it his duty to reprimand the gardener or dismiss him, and there- fore the complainant thought it right to have recourse to the law. The rector was there on the last occasion in the interests of his man. (Mr, Brown: In the in- terests of justice), aid he Mr. Hockin thought that he might be present now in the interests of justice, and he might say that he had written to Mrs. Ray asking her to be present, and had summoned the complainant's fellow servant. The complainant corroborated the statement of Mr. Hockin, and stated that she is now in the service of Mr. Lees of Whitefield. The defendant she said called her all the bad names he could think of. When he first let her go he put his foot out and threw her down on the floor and kicked her. She struggled to get up, when he struck on both sides of her face and head. She seized the "jack" and shied it at him, he having backed into the servants halt, but it missed him. She then tried to make her escape from the kitchen, when he again knocked her down by a blow at the back of her neck, and just as she was on the floor, Mrs. Ray came into the kitchen. Complainant had to go to bed, and was delirious all that night, and remained in bed all the following day. - It transpired that since the summons was served on the fellow-servant, Louisa Cartwright, she had left Mr. Ray's service and gone to live at Ellesmere in Shropshire, from which place she had volunteered to come if complainant would pay her railway fare. The cross-summons was then gone into. James Cartwright stated that when Brandt ordered the potatoes there was a panmug nearly full in the scullery. She told him it was no business of his, and that he wanted the stuff to sell it himself. He told her that she had taken something away that morning which did not belong to her—some flowers. She got "in a wild stupid rage," seized hold of his whiskers, and scratched his face. He pushed her away, and she struck him with the jack. lie was marked on the face and head.—Cross-examined : He did not strangle nor kick her. She tumbled over a chair when he took the jack from her. He was still in the employ of the Rector, and at the time of the assault defendant had been in his service six weeks. He pushed her by the throat. There were marks on her face which he could not understand. That summons, taken out after the hearing of the case, should have not taken place. Thomas Renshaw, under gardener at the Rectory at the time of the affray, deposed to the gardener's face being scratched. Mr. Brown said that his friend had insinuated that there was a conspiracy on the part of his (Mr. Brown's) client's employer, the Rector of Ashton-upon-Mersey, and Mrs. Ray, to screen that ruffian in their employ, and not come there and tell the truth in favour of that unprotected female. That was a rather serious issue, which he had confidence in accepting the Bench's de- cision upon. It was a grass libel on the Rector of Ashton-upon-Mersey, and no advocate, without one tittle of evidence, should infer that the Rector and his wife had connived with that ruffian. Mr. Hockin observed that his ft iend had indulged in personalities, which he could very well afford to treat with the silent contempt they merited. It was not the I first time that he had met Mr. Brown, he having be- fore met him in his native town of Stockport, where what he had said there was simply as mother's milk n comparison with the language he used at Stock- port. He (Mr. Hockin) had therefore for a long time given up answering personalities. Mr. Brown repudiated having uttered any person- alities, and observed that what he said was "as an advocate acting upon the instructions of his client." Mr. Hockin said that if there were no personalities he was pleased to have been mistaken. He purposed calling the Magistrates' Clerk as to the condition of Brandt at the time that she applied for the summonses. No charge would have been brought against Brandt had not that charge been preferred by her against Cartwright. Mr. Brown (to the Magistrates' Clerk).—l know why you are doing this. The Magistrates' Clerk.—You may know what you like. Mr. Brown.—This witness is called at the instance of the Magistrates' Clerk. Mr. Wootton (the deputy clerk).—There is not a shadow of truth in the statement. Mr. Brown.— I heard you mention it to him. The Bench retired, and on returning into court Mr. Worthington, who presided, said the Bench had con- sulted over the cases, and came to the conclusion to dis- miss both of them.

div.head: SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT NORTHWICH
div.p: SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT NORTHWICH
SPORTS.

During the progress of the sports at the fete and flower show held at Wilmington on Saturday last, a serious accident occurred to one of the speetators. During the peny race a dog rushed at one of the ponies, belonging to Mr. Clarke, of Acton Bridge, and caused it to shy suddenly and jump over the outer fencing which bounded the course amongst the alarmed crowd. In its leap the animal struck a man named James Wilkinson in the neck, and felled him. Several doctors who happened to be present were promptly on the spot to afford assistance, and they found that the man's neck was dislocated. He was immediately conveyed to an outbuilding of Wilming- ton Hall, where his injuries received every possible attention. The sufferer was afterwards carried in a vehicle to his home at Acton Bridge, where he still lies in a somewhat precarious condition.

div.head: MORE COCK FIGHTING IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: MORE COCK FIGHTING IN CHESHIRE.

At the Eddiskury Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Dykes, William Grocott, and Henry Grocott, labourers of Beeston, were summoned for cruelty to two cocks. Sergeant Ralph Sontherns stated that on the 24th! June last, he received information that there was a cock fight about to come off. He saw William Grocott coming in the direction of Beeston, with a cock in a bass, along with his brother. Witness afterwards went in the direction of Beaton, and found the three defendante fighting two cocks. He watched them at the back of a hedge for some time. They then went away, and he followed Dykes to his house, and there he found a cock bleeding on a sofa. He took the bird to Superintendent Mayho, and it was then bleeding. The Grocotts went in the direction of Bunbury.— Superintendent Mayho stated that the last witness brought him a game cock. On examining it, he saw it had been fighting, and that it was very badly knocked about the head, and its legs were all covered with blood.—The Hon. A. Laseelies: Was it trimmed? Mayo: No; the comb was cut, but it was not trimmed like these (pointing to two stuffed birds in the room i which bad figured n a noted ease of this description about three years ago.) This bird had good spurs of its own.—Job Williams stated that he was in his house on the day in question, near to Dykes'' whose cock had been accustomed to fight with one he had. Dykes asked him to come and see fair play; but he, thinking Dykes referred to his cock, declined to let them have it to fight. He asked him to take away his cock, and then saw two cocks fighting. He asked them to leave off, and they took up the birds and went away. His bird was not engaged.—The defendants had no wit. flosses, but all asserted that Southern did not see the fight.—Henry Grocott said he would not deny that the birds fought, but it was only a minute or two.— The Hon. A. Lasoelles said there was no doubt the birds were fighting. He didn't think there could be any doubt about the case as far as it went. It was an illegal thing to make two cooks fight. True they were in their natural state, and there was no assemblage to witness the fight.—Henry Grocott Neither of them was twelve months old. The Hon. A. Lascelles : You were just seeing how they would frame? (Laughter.) But you must not cock-fight.—Henry Grocott: It shall not be any more; I have made away with my bird—Dykes ; / was not aware there was any law against this.—The Hon. A. Lascelles This does not seem to have been a regular "main ; " it was only a little skirmish; but you must be warned. You will be fined 7s. 6d. and costs each. We could fine you £5 each.

WARRINGTON AND MANCHESTER. The revival of an old project to make the Mersey navigable from Liverpool to Man- chester is just now receiving some public attention. The financial and en gi eering aspects of this huge enterprise, which it is calculated will require for is execution the formidable capital of three millions and a half sterling, is discussed by the Liverpool Ifercury in the following article :

The often-discusied project of a ship canal between Liverpool and litanchestar having been taken UP by Hamilton Fulton, an engineer of ability and experience deserves to be again carefully and respectfully coll- oid,

tered. But the commercial as well as the engineer- ng questions involved are numerous and difficult, and can only be resolved by the expenditure of many mil- lions on what will to some persons appear a very hazardous experiment. As far as mere engineering is concerned, there is probably no difficulty which Hr. Hamilton Fulton could not overcome. Every mile of the ground is perfectly well known, and is indeed covered or intersected by navigable waters, canals, roads, and railways, constructed or improved by Steers, Brindley, the two Stephensons, and all the other eminent engineers of the last two centuries. So long ago as the reigns of the last Stuart kings and the revolution of 1638, Mr. Thomas Patten, of Bank Hall, Warrington—we believe, an ancestor of Lord Win- marleigh—formed and carried out the great and valu- able object of improving the navigation of the river Mersey from Liverpool to Warrington. About thirty years later, in the reigns of Ueorge I. and 11., the gentlemen of Manchester, with the assistance of Thomas Steers, the engineer of the Liverpool docks, carried out the noble undertaking of rendering the rivers Mersey and Irwell navigable from Warring- ton to Manchester. Again, after an interval of thirty or forty years, that Heaven-born genius Brind with the assistance of the deep purse of the areat Duke of Bridgewater, applied the waters of the Mersey and its tributaries to what he declared to be the real use of rivers, namely, the feeding of navigable canals, and formed between Manchester and Liverpool the Brides-. water canal, joining the Mersey at Runcorn. This was the commencement of the most perfect system of Internal navigation ever formed in this or in any other country. When the railway system was introduced, fifty years ago, it was supposed that canals and navi- gable rivers would be superseded by railways; but that has not proved to be the result, at least in the oases of the Mersey and Bridgewater canal. These great works have been amalgamated with the London and North-western Railway, and that will probably be the result with Mr. Hamilton Fulton's proposed ship canal, if it should be constructed and prove to be profitable to its promoters and useful to the public. But we have seen too much of the difficulty of re- moving a great and firmly established trade from one point to another in the case of Birkenhead, to believe that the trade of the Mersey could be removed from Liverpool to Manchester by the construction of a ship canal between Manchester and Warrington. The present means of transport and communication be- tween Liverpool and Manchester may be regarded as the combined result of the greatest skill of the ablest engineers of the last hundred years, and we should be slow to believe that a ship canal from Warrington to Manchester would supersede them all. The Liverpool docks are free from liability to pay dividends, or a single shilling beyond the cost of construction and man- agement. The proposed ship canal would be a trading company seeking for profit on every transaction, and unable to go on without it. It would, moreover, from the first find itself in close competition with several of the wealthiest and most powerful joint-stock tom- .palsies in the kingdom, which would render its chances of earning a dividend very precarious. In addition to this it must be remembered that Manchester, though the largest, is still only one of at least a dozen large towns and populous districts which carry on trade with the interior and with foreign countri.s through the port of Liverpool. Most of these are situated on the banks of the Leeds and Liverpool canal, or on other parts of the c)alfield of Lancashire, the saltfield of Cheshire, or the woollen district of Yorkshire; and with regard to a considerable part of the goods and produce imported into the Mersey, it is only sent to this country to be exported to other countries.

div.head: MERSEY TO RUNCORN AND WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE MERSEY TO RUNCORN AND WARRINGTON.

The condition of the Mersey and particu- larly of the tidal portion of it, is discussed with the ability which comes of professional skill and euthusiasm in two publications written respectively by Mr. Sames N Shoolbred, members of the Institution of Civil Engineers, and by Mr. Thomas Webs- ter, M.A., F.R.S., eto., and just given to the public, The works are reviewed by a Liverpool contemporary and from that por- tion of the notice which deals with Mr. Shoolbred's paper, we quote the following interesting observations.
It is stated by Captain Foulkes, of Runcorn, for

many years and until lately in charge of the bttoyage of the Upper Mersey, under the Bridgewater Trustees, that the channel up to Runcorn is generally much ire. proved, so much so that vessels of 40 and 600 tons burthen are now able to get up there, while twenty. five years ago none over 250 tons could reach that place. Between Hale Head and Warrington, in 1871, there was a hes of sectional area over what had existed in 1820, but the amount of deterioration was less than in 1861 (12.27 per cent. against 13.48 per cent.), indica- ting an improved tendency during the last decade. Mr. Shoolbred says this state of affairs may, on the whole, be considered satisfactory, seeing that this part of the river forms a species of breakwater whereon the momentum of the tidal wave is expended, and is only partially acted upon by the tide. The flood during spring tides does not last more than three-quarters of an hour at Warrington, while the neap tides affect but little more than the lower half of the district. With reference to this part of the sabject, it may be incidentally observed that until measures are adopted for protecting the property on the margin of the river from waste, and for reclaiming tracts of sandbanks with fascine work or otherwise, it will be impossible to form and maintain permanent deep channels to Garden' Weston, and Runcorn, or to improve the ap- proach to Warrington. With the skilful adaptation of well-known Appliances, it would doubtless be easy to make Warriegton.as accessible as Runcorn now is.

For a period of thirty-three years the annual flower show of the Hale Floral and Horticultural Society has been reearded re one of the thirst displays of floral and vegetable life in the cc ueter, and so assiduously have its promoters laboured that year by year its ex- cellence has increased with its duration. Tide year all former exhibitions were to be eclipsed, over keloo was offered in prizes, and the result was that the num- ber of entries was unusually large in all dep srtnieuts Unfortunately, however, for the success of the project, the heavy rains of the last few days matericl:y inter- fered with the intentions of the competitore, and ruthlessly destroyed the numerous specimens of flowers, fruit, and vegetables, which were as perfect as horticultural skill could make them. Thursday morning opened with weather of the most adverse description. The roio fell in torrents, and during the iuterveniug showers the wind blew in meth gusts as to make it al- most impossible for competitors to forward their contributions with safety. Some, however, were not to be disheartened, and by dint of covered carts suc- ceeded in transferring from greenhouses to the tent erected in the grounds of Hale Hall, the seat of Col. Blackburne, M.P., where the show was to take place, a tolerably large number of valuable plants, and other varieties of the vegetable kingdom, which are required Ito make up an exhibition. The committee, anxious to do their best to make the show a success, had made the most elaborate preparations. Triumphal arches, floral festoons, and displays of bunting, were eeident indications of their desire in this respect, and no doubt had the weather been more favourable,would have con- tributed to the consummation of the committee's desire. The bells of the church also rang out merry peals at intervals, but even a Mark Tapley would have hesitated at feeling jolly while listening to the music of the bells, when drenched to the skin with the pitilese rain. At two o'clock the exhibition opened, and there was a good sprinkling of visitors. The stove :• and greenhouse plants of Mr. H. Crostield, of Liverpo 1, and Mrs. Allison Johnson, of Wootton, were remarkably due, and would have at- tractel attontide, had the visitors had more time to bestow their admiration. Both Mr. Crostield and Mrs. Johnson took Several prizes, and Mr. D. James also took several prizes for his c ellections of greenhouse plants. Mr. John Abbot of Farnworth, and Mr. R. ' G. Morgan were equally successful for their displays of f uschias. The butk of the prizes went to exhibitors from the Liverpool district, the only purely local com- petitor, being Mr. J. Abbot who, as alreauy intimated, t eok prizes in the fuschia class, tee first prize for cucumbers, and the second for asters. The displays of fruit and vegetables were also good, and the exhibi- tion was certainly of a superior character. Before, however, time was given for a complete inspection, the gale assumed alarming proportions, and threatened tee tent with destruction every moment. Additional stakes were put in the ground but without avail, and at three o'clock, one site of the tent succumbed to the effects of the storm, mercilessly crashing plants, flowers, and fruit to the ground. Indescribable confusion followed. Visitors who were in the tent, fled for their lives, and fortunately beyond a little detriment to ladies bonnets and policemens' helmets, they escaped without injury. Eshibitore, naturally alarmed for the safety of their plants, made a general rush to the remaining portion of the tent, and rescued what they could from impending dee- traction. Fortunately for them this effort was made, for in a few moments afterwards the tent fell help. lessly to the ground. Tue sight was really most piti- able. Plants of magnificent foliage, the existence of which would be imperilled by a moment's exposure, and many of them valued at from £5 to £lO each, lay huddled together in hopeless confusion. Flowers of the moat delicate hues, rices and luscious fruit including grapes, peaches, and apricots, lay side by side with broken treepote, scattered vegetables, and displaced timber, the epectacle causing pain to the heart of meny a hortculturalist. A's stance was soon at hand, and the various ex- hibitors picked from the general debris what belonged to them. The committee did all in their p ewer to alleviate the misfortune which had befallen the ex- hibition, but in no way are they responsible for the sad mishap which occurred. Mr. W. H. Abbott, the Sec- retary, Captain D werryhouse, Mr. Amery, and even Colonel Blackbuine himself, did all t 'ley could to protect the plants from further injul y ty gettiag them stowed away in covered carts to SeVe them from the storm. The dams gs cannct be estimated, as time OAR alone repair the effects of the diameter. The greatest consolation te the committee was that the demolition of the mac quee was unattended with per- sonal injury. Notwituetanding the rain, crowds of visitors arrived on the grounds, and were astounded on learning 'he state of affairs. Certainly the most mournful official connected with the exhibition was the mom y taker, for when the tent was bl wie down and its contents removed or /dretroyed, like Othello, his oc• cupstion was Roue. div.head: NEWSPAPER NEUTRALITY WITH
div.p: NEWSPAPER NEUTRALITY WITH
A NEW FACE.
"John Bright and his party have had 40 years out of 4 of power and place, and might have done some- thing to mitigate the sufferings of Dissenters if so

inclined."— Warrington Guardian. THAT enlightened Liberal spirit which, as we have seen, released the Catholics in 1829 from every one of their unjust and in- vidious disabilities, had already directed its attention to the equally grievous political and social exclusion suffered by another great body of Dissenters from the State Church. it is only fair to observe that both the Catholics and the Jews owe their release to the liberal-minded members of both Houses of Parliament, many of them un- connected with party government. While we acknowledge the we come aid at that day of the small Tory contingent, we should be glad to pay a similar compliment to that third party, of which the Warrington Guardian is the official organ, did we know anything about its existence or career as far back as 1830; nor do we hear anything on the subject from contemporary historians. As the London Correspondent of their journal is totally unacquainted with the history of England at that remote period, we must as- sume that the neutral party had not at that time become a power in the State. That it is now a power in the state, we affirm unre- servedly, and with no covert irony, but in all seriousness and sadness. For who can deny that that besotten ignorance and indif- ference, the parent of pauperism and crime, that sleek, self-seeking imposture and vul- gar pretentiousness, are social forces as great as are the highest forms of enlightened culture ; the possession of principles which govern present conduct; the revelation of larger ends, which nourishes hope and in- spires the love of progress towards them. It has been suggested that the London Cor- respondent of the Guardian is identical with a distinguished philosoper of Green- ville, that proud yet popular University which sells its degrees cheaply enough, but yet is rather particular about its customers. We are informed that the Senate adopts the same mode of selection as Madame lus- saud does when she adds to her wax work collection. The elected ones must be pre- eminent in something, although it does not much matter what that something is. In this case the pre-eminence rested presumably on the foundation of a new political party, the discovery of the new doctrine of politi- cal neutrality, which undertakes to teach withoiti knowing, to act without convictions, and in the disguise of journalism and the diffusion of knowledge, to trade upon the ignorance of people, to whom a newspaper has, happily, hitherto been a source at which they might learn both facts an 1 the honest diversity of opinion based upon them.

Before we give an outline of the long and tedious struggle of the Liberal party to ob- tain civil equality and common justice for the Jews, let us observe the alien light in which, in the year 1830, in a ten-fold greater degree than they are now, they were looked upon by our Christian population. The op- position to the Catholic claims was personal, violent and bitter, compared with the stolid resistance to the claims of the Jews. The majority had not dared to pretend that they resisted the Catholic claims from feelings of religious intolerance; they urged that the Catholics were dangerous to the State on the ground of their numbers, their organisatioh, thEir allegiance to a foreign power, the as- cendancy of their priesthood, their peculiar political doctrines, and their past share in the history of England. But the Jews ex- cited no such feelings of jealousy; they were held to be isolated members of a scattered nation, who had no particular attachment to England, who looked upon their co-reli- gionists all over the world as their real com- patriots, and who, in short, as strangers, had no right to a share in our Government. Add to this that Jews themselves are naturally exclusive in their social habits, retiring in their dispositions, in England in a very small minority; and that no powerful organisation asked successive ministers for this redress, and we have reason to be proud of the un- tiring Liberal advocacy, which after nearly thirty years of quiet perseverance finally gained its end, and in 1858, gave to the Jews the full equality of rights which they now enjoy. In the year 1830, the year after the ad- mission of the Catholics to Parliament, a Liberal member introduced a bill for the re- peal of Jewish disabilities. It must be remem- bered that at this time, in consequence of the declaration of allegiance to the Sovereign containing the words "on the true faith of a Christian," a Jew could not hold any office, civil, military, or corporate, He could not follow the profession of the law, as a barrister or attorney: he could neither be a member of Parliament or vote for one. Under these circumstances, the Jewish Disabilities Bill was introduced by Mr. Robert Grant, and supported by Macaulay in his maiden speech. At that time there were only 30,000 in England, yet the Bill was opposed on such grounds as these. They were so rich that tit/ could buy up all the seats in England. Believing in their restoration to Palestine, they were only sojourners here, and could not have any sympathies with the ' people. Then it was said in the same breath that they were too few to be worth regarding but that yet they would overthrow the Christianity of the legislature : that as cer- tain Jews once hated the Founder of Chris- tianity, they would of course try to over- , throw his Church now. Seeing that as long as a man was an unscrupulous hypocrite, there could be nothing to prevent him from taking any oath and office in the land, while the conscientious Jew was excluded from Parliament on account of a difference of be- lief which had nothing to do with the busi- ness of the House; looking at intolerance like this, from the safe refuge of intervening years of Liberal progress, we may well con- gratulate ourselves that the long and tedious battle of religious liberty is nearly fought out.

In 1830 the bill was rejected by the Com- mons : in 1833 it was passed by the Com- mons, but rejected by the Lords: in the following year it met a similar fate. For some years the question was then allowed to rest in abeyance, for it was felt that the Lords were not to be shaken. But while the Jews were knocking at the doois of Parliament in vain, some other of their civil disabilities were removed. In 1839 Lord Denman en:-vted that all persons were en- titled to be sworn in the form most binding on their conscience. lit consequence of this the Jews could be sworn on every oath ex- cepting those which contained the words, "on the faith of a true Christian " ; these words, however, still excluded him from corporate offices and from Parliament. In 1847, to its ever- lasting honour, the city of Loudon returned Baron Rothschild to Pailiament in com- pany with Lord John Russell. Here was an expression of public opinion: the opinion of the wealthiest, the best educated, and the most important constituency in the three kingdoms. As was to be expected, Lord Russell, who was then Prime Minister, sub- mitted a resolution to the House urging that the Jews be placed on the same footing as the Catholics, and again it passed the Com- mons, being supported both by Mr. Ulad- stone and Mr. Disraeli, but it was again ' thrown out by the Upper Chamber. In 1851 Alderman Salomons was returned for 'Greenwich, and although he made even more determined efforts than Baron Roths- child to take his seat and obtain his rights of citizenship and of religious liberty, he was on mole than one occasion removed from the House by the Sergeant-at-Arms, and finally the Court of Exchequer decided that nothing less than a statute would en- able Jews to omit the words which it was impossible they could utter. There was now no hope for the Jews until the Lords could be moved. Baron Rothschild was again and again returned for the City, the people preferring to be temporarily unrepresented to the perpetuation of this senseless in- equality and wrmg. Finally, in the year 1858, a compromise was effected with the Lords. Each Chamber was to frame its own oath, so that at this moment, were the Queen to make a Jew a peer, he could not take his seat, although, happily, this is the only social or political disability (if it can be called one) which he is now under. Th's is a tedious story, and perhaps in reading it, one is as much struck with the obstructive. and incorrigibly narrow and belated assem- blage in the Upper House, as with the un- wearying patience of Liberal statesmen, the perceptible growth of Liberal thought, from year to year, as shown in the increasing majorities of the Commons, and the con- soling fact that in this long contest between reason and power, reason triumphed at last. There is also another lesson to be learnt from the unswerving purpose of the little knot of politicians, who, setting their minds and hearts upon the extension of religious liberty to every man, woman, and child, in the kingdom, vanquished power and preju- 41ice and traditional hatreds, by gradually win- ning over to their ranks, the thoughtless and selfish opposition ranged before them. Deep conviction and passionate singleness of pur- pose was the fuel which fed the enthusiasm which tired them to fight so long and so bravely, and by their speech, their looks, and their newspapers, to spread their spirit, like a splendid infection, throughout the length and breadth of the land. Assuredly no Neutral agency, no not-knowing and therefore not-caring principles contributed to this or any other noble end. The inevi- table Neutrality of ignorance is deplorable wherever it exists, and to inspire a journal with it, if that journal reached the hands of many people, would seem appalling. As it is, one can almost afford to smile at this pic- ture of the blind leading the blind, for the blindness is incurable, and the followers are but few.

div.head: NEWS OF THE WAR.
div.p: NEWS OF THE WAR.

The War in the East absorbs more and more, on each succeeding day, the anxious attention of the whole of Europe, and the daily press of Great Britain abounds with details of the varying fortunes of the ill.matchee_combatants engaged in a terrible and san- guinary struggle ; the one for the prolongation of the terrible VI anny of its unnatural dominion, the other for some tolerable measure of that Freedom which is as the breath cf the nostrils of the people west of Constantinople. At the end of last week it was re- ported that Prince Milan, in view of the Servian losses, requested the Guaranteeing Powers to use their good offices "in order to restore the good understand- ing between himself and the Porte," and to bring about a general suspension of hostilities. The Ptince summoned the foreign consols at Belgrade to a con- ference, and expressed his readiness to negotiate for peace on the basis of the arrangements which were in force before the war. The military honour of Servia had been satisfied by the gallant defence of Alexinatz, and as there was no prospect of a decisive success' it was desirable to prevent the unnecessary effusion of blood. The Consuls gladly undertook to communi- cate this news to their respective governments.

Notwithstanding this the war seems to be proceed- ing with vigour, and it is not considered that it will be ripe for Mediation for some time to come. Public meetings are being held all over England to express popular indignation at the atrocities of the Turks, and to condemn the apathetic action of the English Government in the matter.

At a meeting on the 15th inst., Under the advice of the Town Clerk, the Mayor was requested to call a special meeting of the Ceuncil, to pass a formal resolution, under the com- mon seal of the borough, authorising proceedings by way of injunction against the proprietors of the Spelter Works at Bank Qeay, to restrain them from carrying on their works, on the ground of their creat- ing a nuisance injurious to health and destructive to roperty. Alderman Emma, the chairman of the Sanitary Committee, rose to move the coufirmation of the minutes, and in doing so said a more .disagreeable duty he, perhaps, never had to discharge than to move the confirmation of the minutes of the committee on the present occasion. It was well known that by the Charter of Incorporation the government of the borough was entirely vested in the Corporation, and, that for the more ready discharge of their duties various committees had been appointed. The Sanitary Committee had been formed to look after the health, comfort, and convenience of the inhabitants of the borough; and anything which tended to interfere with these should be firmly yet temperately dealt with. A charge had been brought against the Warrington Spelter Works Company of causing a nuisance which was injurious to health, offensive to the senses, and destructive to property. And as he had stated that it was necessary that all their proceedings should be marked by firmness and temperateness, let them con- sider whether they were justified in asking for the confirmation of the minutes of the committee with re- ference to the Spelter Works. Whilst the public health and convenience were of the first importance, they must not deal with the manufacturing interests of the borough in a light and trifling spirit. (Hear, hear.) It must be borne in mind that the well-beiug of the community, so far as commercial affairs are concerned, rested. almost entirely upon the manufacturing in- dustries .of the place. They could not, therefore, afford to do anything in a trifling manner which should interfere with the legitimate operations of the manufacturer, The Mcklical Officer of Health had stated that the Warrington Spelter Works were the cause of a nuis- ance which was injurious to health, and the gentleman who had acted with him in the matter, Mr. Norman Tate, whose affidavit was not yet in the hands of the Town Council, was of a similar opinion. The com- mittee had also received a memorial signed by up- ards of 160 of the employes of Messrs. Robinson, Son, and Skinner, complaining not only of the offensiveness of the smell from the Spelter Works, but also of pewee and headache which it gave them. The War. rineton Spelter Works, as was well known to every member of the Corporation, had for years been a sub- ject of complaint. The complaint up to a very recent period was of the damage caused to vegetable life. When the works were carried on in Church-street, complaints were perpetual, and since they have been removed to Bank Quay, Cburch-etreet had recovered to a large extent from the injury which it had previously suffered. A new description of work was now carried on, and, if he bad been sightly informed, it was a method by which waste material could be recovered, and by a certain process could be converted into a valuable mercantile commodity. This was the dause of the offensive smell so much complained of.
